Mr; DOUGLAS (Weybum):	Not acting;
he is the minister.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The people will have a say
in that. My recollection of the record of the temporary Minister of Labour is that he was elected first on a labour ticket, but with the assistance of the Liberals. According to my information, all the time he sat in this house he was very nice to our friends across the way. I understand that the last speech he made in this house was a tirade against the people with whom he sat. He went back to his constituency of Hamilton East and ran again on the independent Labour ticket. The Liberals did not contest the election; they gave him their official endorsation, but he was defeated. The people had got wise to him. He is said to be a trade unionist, but everyone who carries a trade union card is not a trade unionist, just as everyone who preaches the gospel of the Toiy party is not a Tory, as is exemplified by their leader, who is now a socialist. That is all I have to say with respect to Mitchell. He has done quite well for himself-

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: We know what labour thinks of him.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: -but not very much for the people who sent him to the house in the first place and gave him a start.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
We have this kind of person in the labour movement. In the final analysis we are all human beings. I may say a little more on this question for the benefit of the hon. member for Edmonton East. I am going to say a little about the administration of the department since the new minister took it over, with relation to Kirkland Lake.
We hear a great deal about planning of industry and the necessity for such planning. It is part of the programme of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. We believe that the industries of this country should be planned and directed in order to give their maximum production. I do not believe maximum production is being achieved at this time. I do not say that because I want to belittle what is being done. We of this group have stated many times that as far as we are concerned we recognize the difficulties of transferring Canada from a peace-time nation to a war-time machine. The Canadians are not a warlike people. They love peace. That was exemplified in our complete disarmament during the years when Hitler was preparing for his onslaught. We realize the difficulties; we know that ministers who have the direction of the war effort are pretty much in our own position; they are ordinary, average people
with not very much knowledge of war or the war machine, or of industry or the planning of industry or its operation; and perhaps they are doing a better job than some of us expected they would. But there are times when we are concerned about the situation.
Take the question of aircraft production. It is admitted that on every front aircraft will be the decisive factor in the war. Yet there is a shortage of planes. We have lost two of our largest battleships in the Pacific because there was not sufficient air support when those boats were out in the narrow straits. So it is rather alarming when we find right here in Ottawa the state of things set out in the Ottawa Journal on January 17. It reads:
Ottawa Car and Aircraft Limited has laid off almost 500 employees in the last six weeks, and many more will be let out soon. Redmond Quain. K.C.. president of the company told The Journal Friday night. While large numbers will be laid off, this condition must not be assumed to be permanent, he said.
Reason for the suspension, Mr. Quain said, was the complete lack of aircraft orders. Drastic reductions in personnel have heen made and will continue to be made because at this particular time the company has no more aircraft orders to fill. . . .
He pointed out that the situation at Ottawa Car and Aircraft Limited was not an isolated case, and that there are other large aircraft factories and companies in a similar position at this time.
Surely, in view of the seriousness of the war situation and the lack of adequate aeroplane support in every area where battles are taking place, a condition of that kind should be inquired into. Why are there no orders for aeroplanes? They want them in Britain; they need them in the United States; we want them here in Canada; they are required in every section of the globe where war is being waged to-day. Yet on January 17 a responsible official connected with aircraft production in Canada makes the statement that there are no orders for aeroplanes and he is laying off men. It is something which should be inquired into and rectified.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It should be censured.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It should be. It appeared in the Ottawa Journal.
These are factors which enter into the question of the conscription of man-power. If you have a job and you are comfortable, and appeals are being made over the radio and in the press for you to enlist, put on a uniform, go to Malaya or some other section, and fight, what is the effect of statements such as the one I have read? I am asked to put on a uniform and shed my blood in some foreign
The Address-Mr. Gillis

country for the protection of Canada. At the same time statements are made that the machines necessary to protect me and enable me to fight that battle are not being produced' in Canada, not because of lack of equipment, of factories, or of employees, but because there are no orders.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
There are too many
factories idle.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Exactly. That is not an inducement to voluntary enlistment. The tendency rather is for one to stay at home where lie is safe-as long as he is safe, however long that may be. There is only one way, in my opinion, to overcome this. I do not say that the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) can do it; he is only one man; I do not say that partisan politicians appointed by the government are in a position to do it, because they are partisan politicians, small-time ward-heelers, and so forth, interested in jobs. These are not the people to step up production and see that these conditions are remedied. You must get someone who is interested in the job, who has some knowledge of what is involved, and who is free from political or any other kind of pressure. I think what should foe done is what Ernest Bevin, the British Minister of Labour, did when he took over his portfolio. It took him just about nine hours in conjunction with his labour advisers to lay down a set of regulations governing war production, and he appointed forty inspectors, men who were capable and competent and could be depended on.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: He picked practical men.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes; and he sent-them into the factories to step up production.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: He is an organizer.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: We, too, have them, but they won't let them organize.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes; that is the trouble.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Some attention should be paid to that. No factory in Canada should be closed which can produce aeroplanes. Every factory should be turning them out.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: They should be working twenty-four hours a day.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Right. And it is essential that we take care of the small details among the people themselves and demonstrate to them that, while we are fighting a war, we still realize that the common people at home are human beings.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: And have to be looked after.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
And have to be looked after. I do not believe that there would be any difficulty in getting men on a voluntary basis in this country if we took care of matters of this kind affecting war production and the everyday needs of the people whom we want to do the fighting. In the final analysis it is the fellow who works who is going to do the fighting. It is not the cabinet minister or the member of parliament. Nor is it the little pin-headed local politician who wants to stay at home and work his machine to death and get what he can out of the war; he should be pushed aside.
There is another matter I should like to bring to the attention of the house, because I think it is retarding enlistments. A committee on pensions sat during the last session of parliament. It was largely composed of members of the government, but two members of our group, of whom I was one, had the privilege of serving on it. A supplementary report was presented to the house, tabled, and, as I understand it, accepted, containing certain recommendations in the interests of men actually engaged in making war. Those proposals were never implemented; they were changed.
One question to which I would direct your attention is the rehabilitation of the soldier after he returns. There is nothing worse, nothing that affects a community more injuriously, than that a man who has made some contribution to the war, who has served perhaps a year, having gone over to England and been returned as physically unfit, should be found walking the streets unable to get a job. He goes to an employer and is told, "Your certificate of discharge is not worth the paper it is written on; you are physically unfit and we do not want men who are unfit." That man is a living example to the other fellow as to why he should not volunteer, and there are many such men. I have run into many of them in my section of the country.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Far too many.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Far too many. The welfare officers working on rehabilitation do the best they can, but they do not get cooperation on that question from the employers, at any rate so far as my part of the country is concerned. We made a recommendation to the pension committee at that time, based on the regulations as they exist now in Britain. It was to the effect that a soldier returning from the war should be retained in uniform for at least six months and given some voca-

The Address-Mr. Gillis
tional training and pay and allowance for himself and his dependents in the meantime, and that he should be rehabilitated and fitted for some gainful employment. That was the committee's report. Now he is put on relief. Under the new regulations he can make application to the welfare officer and be given so much a week for so many weeks or until he is employed.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: There should be no necessity for such relief in a country with the resources that Canada possesses.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is a state of affairs that should be abolished. If we got rid of that condition there would be no necessity for conscription for overseas service. The committee made another recommendation-and these are matters that relate to the war- that the desirability should be considered of extending the provisions of orders in council P.C. 3359 and P.C. 3492 of November 10, 1939, with reference to Canadians serving on ships of other than Canadian registry operating from Canadian ports. That is a question that we considered very carefully. Wherever there is a seaport there is a good deal of trouble in this connection. This has reference to boys serving on convoy ships; and there is no branch of the service that is more essential. They are taking greater chances on old ships than they otherwise would. A lot of these old ships are held together by paint, and they leave these ports loaded with war materials. That is true; hon. members can check it up.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: A little more than paint.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I have seen them in Sydney and even the paint was not holding them together. Everything that will float is put into service, and perhaps that is necessary. But these boys go on board these ships and whereas they have protection if the ship is of Canadian registry-they get the protection of the Canadian pensions regulations-there is no protection whatever for them if they are on a ship of foreign registry-and eighty per cent of the ships leaving Canadian ports are of foreign registry. If they drown, leaving families in Canada, their dependents are out of luck. As I say, there is no protection whatever for them from the Canadian government.
I have received two letters since coming here, one from an old lady of eighty-seven. She brought up a boy from the age of five and he was her only means of support. He tried to enlist in the army but was rejected because he was physically unfit. As his contribution to the war effort he went on board a ship and two days later it was torpedoed and the boy
was lost. There is no compensation for this old lady. Now she has to depend on charity. I have dealt with twenty-five or thirty cases in my own area, because there is a large number of boys from that end of the country going into that service. And without that service there would be no war in England or in any other part of the empire, because they are getting foodstuffs, machinery and other supplies, everything that is produced on this continent which is necessary to carry on the fight over there, by means of these ships. I submit that these boys should be protected by the Canadian government regardless of the registry of the ship.
I have a letter in which I am told that a woman whose husband was lost should look to the Norwegian government for consideration. The Norwegian government is responsible for any compensation to which she may be entitled. But that government is in exile, and that means that this man's dependents are now thrown upon charity-and we know what that is to-day. Something should be done with reference to these little matters, because whether we realize it or not, while people do not publicize these things-and they are not vocal; they have no press in which to publicize them-it is this sort of thing that is eating the core out of the war effort. There is no doubt about that. It is talked about in lodges, in local unions, in fraternal societies and in every avenue through which people congregate in communities. It is reflected in the homes. Boys who should be in uniform, and who would be in uniform perhaps, use this argument. We do not want a repetition of Hong Kong through the closing down of factories. These are problems that we shall have to take care of.
Then there is the question of war-time housing, another important matter. I have had considerable correspondence with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) and with those responsible for war-time housing. In one city I know, the city of Sydney, about a thousand men have been added to the steel plants. There is a steel plate mill opening this month which will require [DOT] 600 more workers. That port is full of ships, and there are thousands of people there who were not in the place prior to the outbreak of war. The result was that when war broke out there was a shortage of housing. They require 500 additional houses. It is impossible to get rooms. The plate mill and the steel plants are essential means of producing war materials and there is resentment in that city in consequence of the overcrowding and the conditions under which people are obliged to live- fifteen persons in two and three rooms.

The Address-Mr. Gillis

Prior to coming here the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and myself, in Sydney, met the mayor and the council and emphasized the seriousness of the unsanitary conditions under which the people were obliged to live owing to overcrowding. That is something that should be looked into and remedied. It retards the war effort and builds up resentment in the minds of the people.
As I have stated on several occasions, the Department of Labour is one of the most important war departments of government. If you will look up the record of the Minister of Labour in Britain you will find that he is the biggest factor to-day over there in the prosecution of the war. The Minister of Labour must have the confidence of those for whom he legislates, and that confidence can be built up only on the basis of his activity and his approach to the people who have to turn out the machines of war.
To date, the Department of Labour has not been functioning as it should have been. I just want to refer briefly to the situation at Kirkland Lake.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I have to inform the hon. member that his time has expired.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Go ahead.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: With unanimous consent.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I will finish as quickly as I can. The Department of Labour bungled the Kirkland Lake situation very badly. The men in that section canvassed all the legal machinery laid down by the government. A government-appointed conciliation board recommended recognition of their union. They were not looking for higher wages or shorter hours or anything impossible. Such matters would have been ironed out later through their agreement; all they asked was the right to sit down round a conference table with the employers and bargain with them as to conditions under which they would work and what wages they would work for. The statement has been made by the new minister that order in council ^685 sets out the principles which the government is supposed to stand for, that labour should be a partner in industry. That is all these men ask for. After canvassing every legal avenue, the operators-they are the saboteurs I talk of-took the position that as far as they were concerned they were not recognizing the government-appointed conciliation board; they were not concerned about the loss to the country; they were a law unto themselves. I pleaded here with the government to take some action to stop what was bound to happen at Kirkland Lake, the men

forced into a strike, that strike with a ballot taken previously, everything done to offset it. Nevertheless the Department of Labour-and I hold them responsible-did not take action with regard to an entire community of between 4,000 and 5,000 people who were earning wages, making a contribution to the war effort of this country, prepared to do anything they could to assist. All they asked was the right to do what the operators had done many years ago, band themselves together for the purpose of mutual understanding and in order to work out their problems on a cooperative and collective basis. That was denied them.
The new Minister of Laibour took charge, and his first official act is one that is not going to stand to his credit, no matter how long he is in that department, if he is lucky enough to go there. He started to handle that question. These men had been on strike for months, living on nothing, there being sent there from other sections of the labour movement to support them money that could have been very well used somewhere else. The heads of the Canadian Congress of Labour in conference just a few days ago with the Minister of Labour thought a solution had been arrived at. The whole matter as far as the union officials and the congress officials were concerned was put up to arbitration, but immediately after coming to that understanding to which the miners of Kirkland Lake agreed, the Minister of Labour did a rightabout face and added a proviso that the men must go back to work in the mines before the dispute would be arbitrated. He did that without any understanding or consultation with either the officials of the union in the Kirkland Lake area or the congress of labour who have offices Tight here in Ottawa. That thing is being further prolonged. I want to make this clear, that while the men have lived up to the laws of this country 100 per cent, the operators have yet to state where they stand on this question and get these men back to work. They are sabotaging that industry; they are violating the laws of this country; they are interfering with the war effort, and as far as I am concerned, if the Minister of Labour was doing his job they should be in an internment camp. That is the unfortunate part; I said, if he was doing his job. There are many men in internment camps in this country for nothing who, if released, would be willing to come out and do some useful job in connection with the prosecution of the war. These people stand out as saboteurs, interfering with the entire life of a community, building up in that section antagonisms and hate and prejudices which

The Address-Mr. Marshall
will not be erased as long as that generation is living there. The men who have gone into the mines against the wishes of the majority of the men with whom they work will never be forgiven or forgotten in that section-; I know, I have gone through that. It will be handed down to them and their children. Laxity on the part of the Minister of Labour ana the government in not seeing that something was done there is responsible for that situation.
I am sorry to have exceeded my time. I have more to say, but I shall reserve it for some other time.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
As I listened to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley), my mind went back over the past ten years, when the movement with which I have the honour to be associated, the Social Credit movement, was so bitterly assailed on all sides. The minister's speech was a masterly defence of the actions of this government. I have a great deal of sympathy for the government now, for we Social Crediters too have borne the burden and heat of the day for an idea. As the Premier of Alberta has said on many occasions, "Truth and Right will prevail." Time alone will prove the wisdom or otherwise of this government's attitude. Posterity will judge.
I should like to compliment the previous speaker, the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), on his splendid presentation.
Three questions, all of them of major importance, have been exercising the minds of the people of my constituency for a long time. The first is, old age pensions, or, Where do the old people go from here? The second is agriculture, or, Where do the farmers go from here? The third is Canada's war effort, or, Where does the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) go from here?
On the question of old age pensions I should like to make just two brief remarks. I hope that ample opportunity will be given early in this session to discuss the Old Age Pensions Act. The action of this government in placing obstacles in the way of bringing some additional measure of happiness and contentment to a section of oUr people is neither appreciated nor deserved. We can find money for mass produced massacre. We can find none for increasing old age pensions. We wrap our cloaks round us and hide behind the law. In Mr. Dunning's time as Finance Minister, lack of money was the excuse for holding up pensions for the blind. Because that excuse would be laughed out of court to-day, we are told that the law stands in the way. I wonder what excuse will be given
next, when this one is finally overcome. I wish to tell this government that this matter of old age pensions is a really live issue. The feeling that a "New Deal" is due for old age pensioners grows and gathers strength. It cannot be lightly brushed aside. It must be faced in the very near future, and faced realistically.
The second1 problem, that of agriculture, is equal in importance to Canada's war effort. We have been told that we are all in the front line to-day, the butcher, the baker, the candlestick maker, the business man, the professional man, and the farmer. An analysis of the economic situation will show that the farmer has appeared in the casualty list more frequently than any other member of organized society. Ninety-nine per cent of the farmers are still on that casualty list. When will this government assume its proper responsibility by taking the farmer out of the casualty column and placing -him where he rightly belongs, namely, in the front line with the rest? I believe now is the time, and this is the place for all members of parliament, particularly those who hail from western Canada, to rise in their places in this house and serve notice upon this government that the wishes of more than 150,000 residents of western Canada who signed a petition, and who are backed by the prayers and good wishes of hundreds of thousands of other Canadians, shall not go unheeded. It is not enough for us as members to offer simply lip-service on behalf of these farmers. We must back up our talk with action, the only kind of action this government in general, and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) in particular, understand; that is, political pressure. A new deal for our farmers, or elsel You may read into this expression what you wish. I mean just what the words are intended to convey; a political threat. We must serve notice that we mean business, serious business. We must not sit complacently in our seats; we must rouse ourselves to action. To me it would be a serious calamity were all the energy, all the labour and all the money poured out by these people to be spent in vain. Ours is a grave responsibility. It will take real courage on the part of Liberal members, particularly, to fight this battle. It must be faced. It must be fought. It must be won. Agriculture must survive.
The third question is the most important one of all. It transcends all others both in magnitude and in importance. The evacua-question of Canada's war effort. The evacuation of Dunkirk; the ebb and flow of the tide of battle in north Africa and Russia; the fall of Hong Kong; the appalling disaster at
The Address-Mr. Marshall

Pearl Harbour, the onward rush of the Japanese hordes in the far east, have done much to awaken our people to a realization of the dangers- which we are facing and which, as Mr. Churchill says, we must face in the future. Our people are stunned by the complacency, by the overconfidence, by the bungling of high military officials, by the red tape, by the departmental jealousies, by the liquor and by the languor, as one financial newspaper puts it, which have brought us time and again to the edge of the abyss. We have made many trips to the edge of that abyss; I hope we shall not fall in.
Is it not time that a thorough house-cleaning was made of those who have been directly responsible for all this bungling? On many occasions in this house we have heard it said, "Let us forget the past." Why should we? We must punish those responsible for our humiliation as an example to those who follow after them. Those in authority at Pearl Harbour were not forgiven. We have had our Hong Ivong. Many brave men lost their lives there. No one, as far as I am aware, paid the penalty for the bungling methods employed. Bureaucracy rules this country, but seemingly bureaucrats are never punished. They have power, with no responsibility. We cannot afford to take chances while the enemy knocks at our gates. I am upset, just as many other hon. members are, at the incidents which have occurred in British Columbia. The dead hand of bureaucracy is seen everywhere. It is little wonder that our people are stunned by the smug complacency in high places.
On every hand people are asking for a total war effort. We, upon whom rests the responsibility of giving the people those things which they demand, must pay some heed to the people. It is not entirely the outbursts of the press that concern me, but rather the smouldering anger of the people who all these years have been kept in the dark.
What is meant by a total war effort? The Prime Minister gave us his definition. It is a thousand pities that he shuns with studied design the question of conscription or national mobilization of finance. My conception of a total war effort is one in which finance and material resources are put into the melting-pot before man-power. May I say, too, that this concept is held by a very large body of public opinion in my constituency. Had finance and material resources been conscripted in the fall of 1939, when we urged this upon the Prime Minister and his government, we would not be in the unhappy position in which we find ourselves to-day. Finance rules the war effort,

ably aided and abetted by a bureaucracy which is growing stronger every day.
One of the speakers earlier in this debate, a member supporting the government, said that this war cannot be carried on without finance. Twisted and distorted thinking hinders rather than assists our war effort. Does my friend not know that, all our leading economists, including such individuals as J. Maynard Keynes, are acknowledging to-day the fact that finance must be made subservient to the wishes of the people. Let my hon. friend go out any day and wave a Canadian government bond for five thousand dollars in front of a Japanese tank, and then come back-if he ever would-and tell us which he found to be of greater importance.
Cassandra, writing in the London Daily Mirror, has this to say about the question of finance:
The news that America is to spend a billion dollars, or is it ten billion?-to suppress Hitlerism is unlikely to send a chill of fear down the Fuehrer's spine.
These vast financial bombshells were impressive about the year 1933, but when Hitler began to demonstrate that fighting power really depended on work, machines and raw materials, the siting began to disappear out of the wads of bank notes and share certificates that the democracies brandished so vigorously.
I don't think any nation can "buy" the defeat of Hitler with its accumulated wealth. You have got to go in and fight the creature.
A ithousand-dollar bill may be a fearsome thing, but I'd be much more scared of a dime's worth of lead coming at me at a thousand miles an hour.
Do not let us lose sight of this simple, realistic fact. We are fighting this war with men and machines, and not with money.
Another speaker

I think he was a member of the Conservative party-remarked that instead of the Prime Minister asking the Canadian people to release him from his 1940 promises, all members of parliament should individually ask their electors to release them from promises made in 1940.
Well, I for one would not wish, nor shall I ask, to be released from any pledges I made in 1940. Early in the war, September, 1939, to be exact, we as a group foresaw that eventually we must face the question of conscription. We might have side-stepped it, but instead we took a determined stand and came forward advocating conscription in the following order: First, finance, second, material resources-these before man-power.
What was the consequence of our stand? Seven seats were lost, because we had the intestinal fortitude to proclaim what actually must be done if we are to give of our very best.

The Address-Mr. Marshall
Subsequent events have proven that we were on sound ground. I wonder what the Liberal senator, who campaigned so vigorously in my constituency during the 1940 election, and who in an unguarded moment told a sympathetic band of Liberal workers in one of our leading hotels that the Camrose constituency was in the Liberal bag because the Social Credit candidate could be tied up to conscription, is thinking about now. If these few remarks meet his eye, I hope he will go back to Camrose constituency and tell the people he was just playing party politics.
This plebiscite is nothing to get excited about. We are overemphasizing its importance. The main thing is, plebiscite or no plebiscite, to get on with the war. From present indications-as witness the appointment of one Charles Bothwell, an ex-member of parliament to the position of chief electoral officer, pro tem, for this plebiscite-it is playing politics. It is a simple means of placing a little more money into circulation by adding to the purchasing power of needy Liberal camp followers. It is a pretence to draw the minds of the public away from the sterner facts of life. It is the simple plan of "spoofing the public," as the Englishman would say.
There is no question about the intention of the Prime Minister. To consult the public on some important issue is a worthwhile thing, and is to be commended. To fiddle while Canada is in flames is an entirely different matter. It seems to me it is the government's desire to draw the attention of the people away from such items as the fiasco of the last victory loan, the war savings racket, the blunders of shipping wheat and scrapiron to Japan, and the present unfortunate situation at Kirkland Lake.
For months past, with the assistance of a high-powered sales organization, we have been bearing down very heavily on those people who have scanty means and slender pocket-books, to get them to invest part of their meagre incomes in war savings certificates and bonds. This branch of our national war effort is bogging down. The sale of these little "two plus two equals five" pieces of paper, which one may see advertised by the brewing industry of Canada on every hoarding in the land, is not going very well. It will take a great deal more persuasion, added to the high-pressure and shady tactics employed by certain types of individuals in the last war loan drive to put the next one over.
The people are becoming educated to this financial racket very quickly.
Leslie Roberts, writing in the January issue of the Montrealer said:
If we are ito move away from the voluntary system under which one man elects to do bis bit by dying in a ditch, and the other by investing his money in war loans at a comfortable rate of interest, only one destination is open to us. That is total war.
Total war means the giving of everything that we have and are, not men, materials and tools, but money, profit and all things which, when added together, comprise the Canadian state. It means the placing of every man and woman in the land on an equal economic footing for the duration of the war, the throwing of everything into the pot.
That is not what the oonsoriptioniists want. What they want is compulsory service for somebody else. Well, until such time as they are ready and willing to give this and more, apoplectic gentlemen whose hardening arteries *render them unfit for battle, and ladies who inundate the letters to the Editor columns (including that great self-naturalized Cana-dienne, Miss Thompson) would be well advised to sing low. By all means give us total war. But let's be done with half-measures designed to restrict sacrifice to age groups.
While I do not agree entirely with Leslie Roberts in all that he has said, yet he has spoken some truths which cannot be glossed over lightly.
By all means give us total war, but do not permit it to become a racket designed to enrich the few at the expense of the many. It is not enough to ask a man to offer his life in the service of his country, only to find on his return that some financial institution has taken possession of his property, and moved his relatives out into the road allowance, as actually happened during the last war.
These financial institutions-soulless organizations-must be made to understand they are in the front line, too. They must be herded there, first, and the sooner this action is taken the sooner shall we have a total-war effort.
The voluntary system of enlistment has not been allowed to function, from the very beginning. It has been hamstrung. Our whole war effort has been marked by blundering, inefficiency, stupidity, sprinkled lavishly with political patronage of the most bare-faced character-bureaucracy on the rampage. From the very beginning recruiting for the army particularly was seriously impaired. Some moron handed the army a battle-dress which the soldiers had to wear on all occasions, especially when off duty. The air force and the navy were both given uniforms of smartness and neatness. I am not quarrelling about the battle-dress, but it was no parade uniform. Everyone knows that. Some person
The Address-Mr. Marshall

is now endeavouring to remedy matters after two and one-half years of war, but the damage has been done. It is almost irreparable. It was an asinine regulation.
Stepping up the pay and allowances of all the forces has not yet been tried. We speak bitterly about the man earning from $5 to $10 a day in industry. We compare his lot with that of the soldier. We do nothing about it. Suggestions are made that the worker in industry must be brought down to the level of the man in the fighting forces; never do we suggest raising the pay of the man in the fighting forces to that of the worker in industry. This type of thinking, the destructive type, is encouraged by those who control the destinies of our nation. They do not sit in the front benches of our government either. Their desire is to keep the people in that state of penury and destitution which will render them more tractable. Increases in pay and allowances will come only when we as members of parliament forcibly demand them.
In 1938 a debate took place between Lord Snell and Mr. Amery over the British Broadcasting Corporation's network. The subject of that debate was, "Should national service be compulsory," and I should like to quote what Mr. Amery said on that occasion:
I am sure that you will agree that nations in the long run depend quite as much upon their civic as upon their military strength, and that the development in their citizens of ever higher spiritual values, is even more necessary to their permanent welfare than are millions of conscripted men with guns and bayonets in their hands. Now those who advocate conscription appear to assume that nations live by guns alone. They wish to take a young man's body and train it for one definite and very limited purpose, while they ignore his other needs as a responsible human personality.
Let me examine very briefly your statement that national defence is a common obligation. I do not deny this obligation, but there is also an obligation to the individual on the part of the state which is rarely remembered. I admit, of course, that all of us as free citizens have some obligation

physical, financial, moral-to the community which has nurtured us and whose social institutions and liberties we have inherited, and historically, of course, there are precedents for enforced military service. In the ancient Greek cities every citizen was compelled to give military service; but the Greek citizen was himself a proprietor who had a direct interest in defending the soil of his fathers, for the land did actually belong to him. The slaves were never called to arms, and no one who had nothing to defend was ever asked to share the risks and burdens of war. Rome acted in the same way. Her armies were armies of citizen proprietors. Nearer our own time, the French revolution was the first to decree a general levy on the ground that the fatherland was .in danger but before doing that, the convention enfranchised the serfs and gave to all the right of property.

If the state considers that there is a responsibility due it from the individual, surely it is not too much to expect that the individual has certain rights and privileges which must be recognized by the state.
The Prime Minister should tell the country, even at this late date, that in future all the men in the fighting forces and their dependents shall be forever economically secure. A statement of this sort would be most assuring to our young men in the armed forces and, in my opinion, would stimulate recruiting to a remarkable degree. You -must offer them more than a farm mortgaged to the hilt and controlled by the financiers of Toronto, or a home where the bailiff's shadow casts gloom and despondency around. It is not enough.
Parliament exists to carry out the wishes of the people. If I interpret the wishes of the people of my constituency correctly, they are for a total-war effort. Thus far these wishes have been thwarted by the bureaucrats of the East block who have given the people what they (the bureaucrats) think is good for them.
For a long time I have entertained the feeling that we must hear what our experts have to say about the whole business-McNaugh-ton of the army, Breadner and Bishop of the air force, Nelles of the navy, and not what the bureaucrats have to say. General McNaugh-ton is now in Canada. Let us summon him before the bar of this parliament to give us a frank statement as to Canada's preparedness and Canada's need for men. This and this alone will satisfy and perhaps allay the fears of our people.
In conclusion, let me summarize briefly. First, this plebiscite will settle nothing, not even the question of compulsory national service. Second, we are playing politics when in reality we should be fighting a war. Third, total-war effort must include conscription of finance and material resources before man-power. Fourth, the bureaucrat must give place to the expert who alone knows how wars are won and lost.	.
If we do not insist on a programme which will give us an all-out war effort, then the letters which we have a right to affix to our names, instead of standing for member of parliament will take on their true significance, a mess of pottage.
On motion of Mr. Fraser (Northumberland) the debate was adjourned.

At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
